key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration as the sole basis for the conviction, supported by the presence of kerosene residue on the victim's garments and the FSL Report.
witness_credibility: The court noted that the witnesses who carried the deceased to the hospital turned hostile, but this did not undermine the credibility of the dying declaration as the circumstances strongly supported the version given in the declaration.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 29.12.1998; Trial judgment: 03.11.2003; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: APRIL 19, 2011
legal_representation: Ram Lal Roy for the Appellant; Gurudatta Ankolekar, Azeem Kalebudde, V.N. Raghuparthy for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The investigating officer did not make any attempt to get recorded the second dying declaration of the deceased by a Magistrate
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 302; High Court: Upheld the conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant poured kerosene on his wife's body and set her on fire, and that the dying declaration recorded by the police officer and endorsed by the doctor was sufficient to convict the accused.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the investigating officer did not make an attempt to record the second dying declaration of the deceased by a Magistrate.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction if it is corroborated by other evidence and the circumstances support its authenticity.
